gold.text: "Take my fourth westernmost symbol" , he told the AI. "Take the best sixteen strategies that you can come up with. Construct near that symbol a factory capable of executing each of those strategies. It should be activated by a glider coming in from the southwest, and the exact strategy chosen should depend on the type of glider and the time it hits. Then, near my second westernmost symbol, make that glider. Allocate eighty percent of resources this intervention turn to this."

The factory picked a strategy that was none of the four that Bai's AI had focused on planning for. And it was coming from a place that Bai had not expected: the halfway point between the center of the board and the northern edge. The factory quickly started generating symbol-carrying spaceships that began to move toward the east, and a storm of gliders that moved north, and then bounced off of rock formations and Bai's own walls to move toward the west. Bai, and her AI, were caught completely by surprise.

Bai's AI also focused on increasing defenses across her own western flank. Zei's *first* gamble paid off, he realized: Bai herself did not realize just how much damage she had done on the west side, and just how little Zei had done to compensate. And so neither she nor her AI realized that by this point, Zei's fourth westernmost symbol could be in the middle of the field.

gold.text: tie dun Or actually, on second thought, he won't answer. But tell him that randomly flipping the least-significant bits, the strategy that everyone always reaches for when they encounter this problem for the first time, is not the ideal solution. Sometimes higher-order bits are totally fine to flip, and sometimes flipping even a least-significant bit is dangerous. What you want to do is: * Train a language model on the actual distribution, so that conditional on what all the other bits are, it can give you probabilities for whether a given bit should be 0 or 1 * Split the data up into buckets - make sure to use the decryption key itself to choose the buckets randomly - and require the bits in the i'th bucket to XOR to the i'th bit in the ciphertext. Within each bucket, use the model to determine which bit's probabilities are closest to 50/50 - meaning both values are "natural" for that bit to have in that context - and flip that bit to make the bucket XOR correct. So you're letting the LLM decide which bits are "least significant" and okay to flip, instead of just always taking the lowest-order binary digit in each number. → Deluin be

"Okay, now I wonder if that was me. I told Deluin to tell the soldier to train an LLM on his own health data and then modify the health data that he is sending out in-flight by flipping the bits that the LLM says are safest to flip, and using XOR over buckets to encode the message so he has a lot of freedom in choosing which bit to flip. Much better for reducing the 'suspiciousness' per bit of hidden data encoded, so he could afford to hide more data inside the same cover traffic."
